tldr: This paper demonstrates that transmitting detailed contact deformations from a robot fingertip directly to a human operator's fingertip with high spatial resolution substantially removes teleoperation awkwardness, bringing movements much closer to smooth, natural human behavior.
hero_caption: Overview of this study and the experimental system. Alongside bilateral force feedback, localized contact deformation patterns captured by the remote robot's vision-based tactile sensor (GelSight Mini) are rendered in real time onto the operator's fingertip via a 32-DoF tactile display. As the spatial resolution of tactile feedback increases (Off → 1D → 2D → Full), teleoperated trajectories converge toward natural trajectories produced by direct bare-handed manipulation.
overview:
Teleoperating robots to perform complex tasks and using that demonstration data to train autonomous robot AI (imitation learning policies) is expanding rapidly. However, teleoperated robots are often much slower and more awkward than humans working with their bare hands. While conventional bilateral teleoperation systems provide pushback forces (force feedback), they lack the cutaneous sense of "where and how contact occurs across the fingertip" (spatially distributed tactile feedback). Operating without this is like working with a locally anesthetized hand: operators constantly hesitate, overshooting targets and making frequent corrective switchbacks.

To address this, the authors built a system that translates contact images from a vision-based tactile sensor on the robot's fingertip into localized dome deformations on a 32-DoF tactile fingertip display driven by electro-osmotic pumps, faithfully reproducing the deformation on the operator's fingertip skin. Keeping bilateral force feedback active, they tested four levels of tactile resolution: "None (Off)," "Uniform across the display (1D)," "Top/bottom split (2D)," and "Fully localized (Full)" across two tasks: discriminating closely spaced buttons and dynamic peg rolling.

Under full spatially distributed tactile feedback, the trajectory deviation from bare-handed manipulation (measured by DTW distance) decreased by up to 79%, drastically cutting down on unnecessary corrective motions such as overshoots and reversals. Furthermore, the operators' perceived mental demand dropped significantly, and the variance across collected demonstration data (state-space dispersion) became much tighter. This work clearly shows that reproducing spatial touch at the fingertip is essential for intuitive teleoperation and collecting high-quality, human-like demonstration data.
contributions: Developed a teleoperation system integrating bilateral force feedback with a 32-DoF high-density cutaneous display to directly reproduce localized contact deformations from a remote robot onto a human fingertip.

Quantified movement naturalness (proximity to bare-handed trajectories) using Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) beyond simple speed and success metrics, showing that higher tactile spatial resolution restores natural human motor patterns.

Demonstrated that spatially distributed tactile feedback reduces operator trial-and-error and hesitations, yielding compact, consistent demonstration trajectories that directly improve learning efficiency in imitation learning.

sections.heading: Why Force Feedback Alone Isn't Enough: The Need for Spatial Touch at the Fingertip
sections.summary: Humans rely heavily on fine contact locations and pressure distributions felt across fingertip skin to move effortlessly. Traditional teleoperation emphasizes force feedback, but without spatial cutaneous sensations, operators move awkwardly, much like working with anesthetized fingers.
sections.details:
When reaching for a cup, a human hand follows a clean, bell-shaped velocity profile, grasps without overshooting, and lifts with just enough force to prevent slipping. What underpins this smooth, dexterous movement is the dense network of cutaneous mechanoreceptors distributed across the fingertip. When fingertip skin is anesthetized and deprived of touch sensations, humans become remarkably clumsy, often applying excessive force that risks crushing objects or over-relying on vision to avoid drops.

Exactly the same issue plagues robotic teleoperation. While bilateral control transmitting gross interaction forces has been studied for decades, spatially distributed cutaneous feedback—such as contact patch spread or micro-slips—has been missing. As a result, human teleoperators make excessive corrective actions, leading to slow and unnatural movements compared to bare-handed manipulation. Recently, training autonomous policies (imitation learning models) from teleoperation demonstrations has gained huge momentum; however, if demonstration quality (naturalness and consistency) is poor, the learned policies inherit those same awkward behaviors.

Previous sensory substitution approaches used vibrations, skin stretch, or tilting fingertip platforms, but these compress spatially distributed contact down into 1D or low-dimensional signals. In this work, the authors tested whether an electro-osmotic 32-DoF tactile display that directly renders localized fingertip deformations could restore natural human motor patterns.

sections.heading: Button Discrimination: One-Shot Presses Without Overshooting, Even Blindfolded
sections.summary: In a blindfolded button discrimination task with buttons spaced just 1 cm apart, high-resolution tactile feedback significantly reduced overshoots and switchbacks, producing near-straight, natural trajectories comparable to direct bare-handed operation.
sections.details:
In the first experiment, 12 blindfolded participants performed a discrimination task where they had to press a designated button out of two placed only 1 cm apart. Because the robot fingertip (2.5 cm wide) was wide enough to cover both buttons at once, pinpointing which part of the fingertip contacted a button edge demanded high spatial accuracy.

The experiment tested four tactile feedback conditions:
- Off: No cutaneous feedback (force feedback only)
- 1D: The entire display expands uniformly upon contact
- 2D: The top or bottom half of the display expands independently depending on contact location
- Full: Localized dome deformations matching the sensor image (individual control of 32 actuators)

The results were dramatic. In the Off condition, operators frequently overshot the target and made repeated back-and-forth switchbacks to locate the button. While 1D and 2D feedback improved performance, participants still exhibited detours—often overshooting first and then correcting back to confirm the button. In contrast, under the Full condition, these extra detours vanished, producing ballistic trajectories that closely matched bare-handed manipulation.

Evaluating trajectory similarity against the bare-handed baseline using Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) revealed that DTW distance decreased significantly as feedback resolution increased ($p < 0.001$). In particular, the Full condition significantly reduced DTW distance compared to 1D ($p = 0.014$), while also minimizing trial-to-trial trajectory variance (standard deviation). While overall completion time was also substantially shortened by tactile feedback, the difference in completion time between 1D and Full did not reach statistical significance; however, in terms of trajectory naturalness, Full resolution made a decisive difference.

captions.P6: Experimental results for the button discrimination task. (A) Overview of the blindfolded task to discriminate between two buttons spaced 1 cm apart. (B) Representative trajectories under each feedback condition (red: bare hand, solid lines: with tactile feedback, dashed lines: without tactile feedback). As tactile resolution increases, switchbacks and overshoots disappear, converging to bare-handed trajectories. (C–F) Comparisons of overshoot magnitude, DTW distance, DTW standard deviation, and completion time. The Full condition minimizes both unnecessary corrections and variance.

sections.heading: Peg Rolling: Eliminating Finger Slips and Extending Stroke Length in Dynamic Tasks
sections.summary: In a dynamic peg-rolling task, higher-resolution tactile feedback allowed operators to accurately track the contact point between the finger and peg, virtually eliminating finger slips and completing the roll in fewer, longer strokes.
sections.details:
To determine whether benefits extend beyond static discrimination to dynamic manipulation, 10 participants completed a peg-rolling task: rolling a cylindrical peg forward to a front stop and then back to a rear stop. This task requires alternating between forward rolling "strokes" and lifting the finger back in "loopbacks."

Rolling efficiently requires sensing exactly how far the peg has traveled along the finger pad, rolling it to the limit, and repositioning the finger by the correct amount. Under the Full condition, participants achieved significantly longer travel distances per stroke (mean stroke length, $p \le 0.004$) and required the fewest strokes to finish the task ($p \le 0.014$).

By contrast, with low tactile information (1D and Off), operators were uncertain about where the peg was on the fingertip, frequently rolling past the edge and slipping off the peg onto the floor. In the Off condition especially, participants misjudged finger reset distances, repeatedly losing the peg and making wasted, empty motions. For both bare-handed DTW distance and completion time, the Full condition clearly outperformed 2D and 1D ($p \le 0.003$), while also keeping intra-operator variance lowest.

sections.heading: Lower Mental Load: Freeing Operators from Decoding Clunky Signals
sections.summary: Post-experiment NASA-TLX surveys revealed that operators' perceived mental demand steadily decreased as tactile feedback resolution increased, confirming that natural sensory feedback alleviates cognitive load.
sections.details:
When participants rated their workload across conditions using 7-point NASA-TLX scales, the results revealed a striking trend. As tactile resolution increased, not only did subjective performance improve, but mental demand (Q2), perceived task difficulty (Q3), and frustration (Q4) consistently declined.

Notably, mental demand decreased significantly with each resolution step: Off to 1D, 1D to 2D, and 2D to Full ($p < 0.05$). This indicates that when given low-dimensional, impoverished tactile signals (such as uniform vibrations or half-pad inflation), operators had to consciously interpret and translate what the cue meant, incurring a heavy cognitive cost.

Conversely, when fingertip deformation was faithfully mirrored at high resolution, operators could tap directly into the subconscious sensorimotor loops used in daily life, moving their hands intuitively without deliberate overthinking. The simultaneous recovery of trajectory naturalness and reduction in cognitive load demonstrates that this system harmonizes seamlessly with human biological control mechanisms.

sections.heading: Benefits for Robot Imitation Learning: Tighter Datasets and Higher Quality Demonstrations
sections.summary: Analyzing the distribution of teleoperated demonstration trajectories revealed that spatial tactile feedback dramatically compresses state-space occupancy. Even across operators with varying skill levels, data consistency is preserved, yielding ideal demonstrations for policy learning.
sections.details:
In imitation learning for robotics, it is well established that demonstration datasets occupying narrower, more consistent regions of state space lead to better learning efficiency and generalization. Accordingly, the authors analyzed the consistency of all collected trajectories.

State-space heatmaps for the peg-rolling task showed that without tactile feedback, trajectories scattered widely due to slips and hesitant corrective moves. In the Full condition, however, trajectories clustered tightly around the ideal path. Intra-operator DTW distances between trials were significantly lower under the Full condition ($p \le 0.003$).

Even more critical is consistency across different operators. Participants ranged from complete teleoperation novices to experienced users; yet in the multi-operator dataset pooling all users, pairwise DTW distances were significantly lower under the Full condition than any other ($p < 0.001$), showing remarkable uniformity. Providing spatial tactile feedback allows even beginners to avoid failed corrective maneuvers and produce compact trajectories similar to experts, proving its immense value as a data collection tool for robot learning.

sections.heading: Discussion: Matching Feedback to Task Dynamics and the Value of Movement Naturalness
sections.summary: The benefits of spatial tactile feedback depend on how redundant it is with force feedback and the feature scale of the object. Supplying spatial information that complements force feedback is critical, and achieving movement naturalness is a vital metric in its own right.
sections.details:
An intriguing takeaway is that the benefits of spatially distributed tactile feedback depend on the task. In peg rolling, uniform 1D feedback essentially duplicated the bulk interaction forces felt as the peg pushed against the finger, resulting in little improvement over the Off condition. Marked improvements appeared only when spatial location cues—which force feedback cannot convey—were introduced (2D and Full). While sensory substitution often employs uniform tactile cues to replace force, conveying independent spatial information is where tactile feedback truly shines.

The relationship between object feature size and feedback resolution also became clear. In the button discrimination task, because the button was very small, only a few display pixels engaged in the Full condition; some participants found the larger active region in the 2D split condition more intuitive. Tactile rendering resolution must therefore be designed around the spatial scale required by the task.

Finally, this study showed that completion time and trajectory naturalness can improve independently. Even when completion times are comparable, eliminating wasteful reversals and overshoots to recover bare-handed motor patterns directly reduces operator fatigue and weeds out harmful noisy maneuvers from imitation learning datasets.

sections.heading: Under the Hood: Integrating High-Density Tactile Sensing with Micro-Actuators
sections.summary: Using a custom 2-DoF leader-follower teleoperation setup, real-time image processing binarized contact images from a GelSight Mini sensor into 32 contact zones, mapped without noticeable delay to micro-domes powered by electro-osmotic pumps.
sections.details:
### Hardware Architecture
The setup utilized a custom 2-DoF (horizontal and vertical) leader-follower telemanipulator. Each axis was driven by a brushless DC motor via a capstan drive, with position measured by 14-bit optical encoders. A microcontroller (Teensy 4.1) ran a high-speed 10 kHz bilateral position-force control loop, providing stiff force feedback of 9.4 N/mm vertically and 2.2 N/mm horizontally. A compact vision-based tactile sensor (GelSight Mini) was mounted at the follower robot's tip.

### Tactile Display and Mapping Pipeline
A 32-DoF tactile skin-deformation display by Fluid Reality was positioned on the operator's fingertip. Elastic domes arranged at a 3 mm pitch are individually inflated by embedded electro-osmotic pumps.
- Sensor image processing: The difference image $I_d$ relative to an initial reference frame $I_0$ is converted to grayscale and smoothed with a Gaussian filter.
- Noise thresholding and binarization: When the Frobenius norm of the difference image exceeds a noise threshold $T_{\text{noise floor}}$, Otsu's thresholding is applied.
- Display mapping: For local regions of radius $r$ centered at each actuator coordinate $(x_i, y_i)$, if the Frobenius norm of pixel intensity exceeds a contact threshold $T_{\text{contact}}$, the corresponding dome is pressurized and inflated.

As a baseline, participants were blindfolded with their index finger attached directly to the follower tip to record natural bare-handed trajectories. Comparing teleoperated trajectories against these baselines via DTW provided an objective quantification of naturalness.

takeaways: In robotic teleoperation, transmitting localized skin deformation alongside force feedback is key to restoring human dexterity and smooth motor patterns.

Spatially distributed tactile feedback not only accelerates task completion, but also eliminates unnecessary corrections like overshoots and hesitations, significantly lowering operator mental workload.
Because it generates clean, converged trajectories, spatial tactile feedback greatly improves the consistency and quality of demonstration datasets collected for robot imitation learning.
Higher tactile resolution is not universally better; display resolution must be thoughtfully matched to the target object's feature size and the degree of redundancy with force feedback.
limitations: The experimental setup was limited to planar 2-DoF single-finger manipulation; validation on complex 3D contact tasks, such as multi-fingered dexterous grasping and in-hand manipulation, remains future work.
Trajectory naturalness was evaluated by DTW distance on position trajectories, which does not fully capture long-horizon behavioral transitions or multi-joint kinematic coordination.
While cognitive demand reductions were demonstrated during experimental trials, the long-term impact on operator fatigue and device durability over extended work sessions was not directly measured.
